Row.Text: Emigration

Citizens emigrate from unhappy, struggling cities to happier, more prosperous ones, both within and between civilizations, driven by a Prosperity model (food, production, happiness, war, siege, starvation). Migration counts are reported as historically representative populations, aligned with the Demographics mod's scaling.

Pressure needed to emigrate
Pressure a settlement must build before one population point emigrates. Lower = more frequent emigration.
Pressure kept each turn

How much of a settlement's built-up emigration pressure carries over to the next turn. Below 1 the pressure falls again when conditions improve, so a settlement that has recovered stops drifting toward a departure; the lower the value, the faster it forgets. At 1 pressure only ever rises until someone leaves.
Reasons to stay: {1_List}
Size dilutes prosperity

How much a settlement's own size divides away what it produces. At 1 prosperity is a straight per-citizen average, so a large settlement can never out-build its size. Lower values let a big settlement keep more of what it has built.
Buildings are a reason to stay
Counts what a settlement has, such as wonders, a granary, a market, a school or walls, as a reason to stay, on top of what those buildings produce. Each kind counts once, however many there are.
Most a settlement's buildings can hold
Ceiling on how much a settlement's wonders and buildings can add to its appeal, so a long build order strengthens a place without putting it permanently out of reach.
Reluctance to move somewhere smaller

Friction per population point when the destination is smaller than the settlement being left, the mirror of the crowding friction for moving somewhere bigger. At 0 nothing resists people draining out of a large settlement into its lesser neighbours.

Most departures per city per turn

The most population points one settlement can lose to migration in a single turn. This is the direct cap that stops a city emptying out during a siege. Deaths are a separate channel, not counted here. The intensity preset sets this (Low 1 / Medium 2 / High 4).
Most arrivals per city per turn

The most population points one settlement can gain from migration in a single turn. This is the symmetric cap that stops a single boomtown absorbing dozens of migrants at once. The intensity preset sets this (Low 2 / Medium 4 / High 8).
How often migration runs
Run the emigration pass once every N of your turns. Raise it to ease per-turn cost on large saves, and, if the Demographics mod is installed, lower its sample frequency first.
Migration between civilizations
If off, people only move between cities of the same civilization.
Include city-states and minor powers
Whether minor / city-state settlements take part in migration.
Only civilizations you have met
Only consider foreign cities your civilization has met.
Leader and civilization traits

Apply small, hand-tuned per-leader and per-civilization adjustments (magnet damping, integration speed, war-time retention, source bias) so outliers behave distinctly. Off = every civilization uses the same global model.
Strength of leader and civilization traits

How far the per-leader/civ adjustments are allowed to diverge from the global model. 1.0 = full distinct identities; lower values flatten the differences between civilizations toward the same model to curb snowballing; 0 = fully flat (same as turning the table off).
Use border policies
Enable the Pro- / Anti-Immigration Stance cards' effect on immigration (the cards are added in the policy menu and cost or grant Influence). Off = the stances have no migration effect.
Anti-Immigration: immigration let through

How much immigration the Anti-Immigration Stance lets through (0.4 = about 60% turned away, and any refugees you do admit settle more slowly). Lower = more closed. Only used when border policies are on.
Anti-Immigration: pull of rival civilizations

How strongly the Anti-Immigration Stance keeps your own people from leaving for rival civilizations (0.6 = their pull toward other civilizations cut to 60%; 1 = off). Lower = stronger retention. Only used when border policies are on.
Pro-Immigration: immigration boost
How much the Pro-Immigration Stance increases immigration (1.5 = +50%). Higher = more open. Only used when border policies are on.
Weight of food per person
How much per-capita food pulls migrants toward a city.
Weight of production per person
How much per-capita production (the "work available" proxy) pulls migrants.
Weight of happiness
How strongly a city's net happiness attracts migrants.
Penalty for city size
How much a city's size counts against it (so small thriving towns still attract).
Shaped happiness model

Replace the flat happiness weight with a nuanced model: happiness is measured against the world average, a happy city's pull levels off (no runaway magnet) while misery still strongly repels, and happiness amplifies a city's economy instead of dwarfing it. Off = the simpler flat happiness weight.
Shaped model: happiness saturation
How many points above the world-average happiness count as "very happy" before the pull saturates. Higher = happiness keeps mattering longer. Only used by the shaped model.
Shaped model: economy amplification
How much a happy city's economy is amplified (and a miserable one suppressed) as a migration draw. Only used by the shaped model.
Overcrowding discount
Credit back some of the unhappiness a city suffers purely from urban overcrowding, so a deliberately tall/dense city isn't double-punished (its density already suppresses its yields). 0 = off.
Urban population before overcrowding
Urban population a city can hold before overcrowding counts against it (mirrors the game's overcrowding threshold). Only used when the discount is on.
Emigration per point of violence
Score penalty per point of accumulated combat intensity in a city's borders.
Largest violence penalty
Ceiling on the violence penalty, so a rout saturates rather than runs away.
Violence kept each turn
How fast accumulated violence fades with no new fighting (lower = fades faster).
Violence before refugees flee
Minimum violence before refugees flee directionally away from the nearest enemy.
Weight of fresh city damage
Intensity added when a city takes new district damage in a turn (an assault spike).
Weight of an ongoing siege
Intensity added each turn while a city center stays damaged.
Weight per pillaged tile
Intensity per pillaged improvement in a city's borders, per turn. 0 skips the scan.
Siege model (capped and escalating)

Make war-driven emigration escalate the longer a city is besieged, but cap the total a city can lose to war so it can't be fully depopulated without a capture (the remnant digs in). Off = the simpler flat violence penalty.
Siege: time to full pressure
How many turns a siege must last to reach its full emigration pressure (a fresh raid starts gentle and ramps up). Only used by the siege model.
Siege: most of a city lost to war
The most of a city's population (as a fraction of its size when the siege began) that war-driven emigration can take before it stops. Only used by the siege model.
Most refugees leaving in one turn

The most rural population a heavily besieged city can shed in a single turn. War refugees then leave in bursts that scale with the intensity of the fighting, instead of a steady one-per-turn trickle, still bounded by the siege loss cap. 1 = off (the old trickle).
Refugees avoid the attacker

How strongly refugees fleeing a war avoid the civilization that attacked them, preferring their own cities first, then any third party, and the aggressor last. 0 = off (refugees ignore who started the war).
Refugees prefer their own civilization
How strongly war refugees prefer to resettle within their own civilization before crossing to another. Only used when "Refugees avoid the attacker" is on.
Distance penalty per tile
Pull penalty per hex between source and destination. Higher = more local migration.
Refugees flee away from invaders
How strongly refugees prefer destinations away from the nearest invader.
Reluctance to cross a border
Extra reluctance to migrate across a civilization border.
In a crisis: flee abroad

How strongly a civilization in acute crisis (war/disaster) pushes its refugees to flee ACROSS BORDERS to another empire, rather than relocating to its own (equally-stricken) cities and dying there. Higher = more cross-civ escape. 0 = off.
Open Borders agreement boost
How much a base-game Open Borders agreement between two civilizations eases migration between them, both directions. 0 = off.
Longest time in transit

The longest a migrant can spend traveling before arriving. They leave the source the turn they depart; the actual delay scales with the distance to their destination (farther = longer), up to this cap. War refugees always take at least a turn. If their destination is destroyed while they are en route, they perish in transit. 0 = instant arrival.
Integration load per migrant

Integration "load" added to the receiving civilization for each migrant it absorbs. The civilization pays a per-turn cost proportional to its current load, which decays over the integration duration. 0 = off.
Extra load in large settlements
Multiplies the load added by (1 + this × destination population), so absorbing into a large settlement adds more. It brakes runaway population magnets.
Integration load kept each turn
How fast the integration load fades each turn. This sets the duration of the cost. Lower = shorter (migrants integrate faster); higher = the cost lingers longer.
Celebration delay per unit of load

Happiness taken from the civilization's celebration progress each turn per unit of integration load, so absorbing migrants delays its next Celebration. It does not make any settlement unhappy (the game exposes no way to do that). 0 = off.
Gold per turn per unit of load
Gold drained each turn per unit of integration load, including across civilizations. 0 = off.
Celebration delay per unsettled migrant

Happiness taken from celebration progress each turn per held migrant a civilization has not yet settled, scaling with the count, so overflow migrants must be settled, not hoarded. Delays the next Celebration; never makes a settlement unhappy. 0 = off.
Gold per turn per unsettled migrant
Gold drained each turn per held migrant a civilization is holding, scaling with the count. 0 = off.
Departures abandon a rural tile

When people leave a settlement, one of its outlying rural improvements is abandoned along with them, so the settlement really loses that tile's yields. Applies to every civilization. Off = the population count drops but every tile keeps working.
How newcomers settle

Off: the game's own Grow City prompt asks you to place each point. Automatic: the city places it at once. Ask me: a pop-up lets you choose the tile, let the city decide, or wait. Migrant unit: newcomers arrive as a Migrant unit you resettle yourself. Other civilizations always place their own arrivals.
Ask about refugees

In Ask me mode, raise the Newcomers pop-up when refugees settle in your cities: people fleeing war, disaster, famine, or conquest, and refugees leaving resettlement. Off = the city places them at once.
Ask about migrants
In Ask me mode, raise the Newcomers pop-up when migrants settle in your cities: people who moved for a better life. Off = the city places them at once.
Ask about returnees
In Ask me mode, raise the Newcomers pop-up when people return home from abroad to your cities. Off = the city places them at once.
Prefer specialist slots
When newcomers are placed automatically, seat them as a specialist in a district that has room before improving a rural tile. Specialists yield more but cost the settlement food and happiness upkeep.
Most of a settlement one disaster can drive out

Across one disaster crisis (until its distress fades) a settlement loses at most this share of the population it had when the crisis first cost a point; the remnant digs in. The disaster twin of the siege cap.

Pressure from wars with major civilizations
How much conflict pressure an attack creates when a major civilization is among the attackers. 1 is the default; lower means wars displace fewer people, higher means more.
Siege floor: major civilizations
Pressure a city merely besieged by a major civilization feels before any real damage. Actual damage always counts in full.
Pressure from raids by minor powers
How much conflict pressure a city-state or Independent Power attack creates, against a major civilization's war. Lower means their raids displace far fewer people.
Siege floor: minor powers
Pressure a city merely besieged by a minor power feels before any real damage. Actual damage always counts in full.
Call people home

Offers a paid call to bring displaced people back to the settlement they fled, in a size you choose. From your own settlements it is a purchase: that many come. From abroad the call is paid for either way and each person asked may or may not answer.
Offer when things are calm
Raises the call automatically once no settlement of yours is under war, siege, disaster or famine and your people are still displaced. Off leaves it to the console.
Chance each point returns from abroad
How likely each point living under another civilization is to answer a call. Low: they have a life there now, and a call may bring nobody.
Gold to call one person home
The Gold price of a call for one person. Bigger calls climb faster than the head count (two cost about 2.8 times this, three about 5.2 times), and calls abroad are scaled up on top.
Influence to call one person home
The Influence price of a call for one person, on the same curve as Gold.
Price climb per age
Every age past Antiquity multiplies the price of a call by this, so a call keeps its weight as treasuries grow: at 3, an Exploration call costs 3 times the Antiquity price and a Modern call 9 times.
Most population points per call

Congestion brake

Make a civilization that's absorbing lots of migrants a less attractive destination for further migration (it's busy integrating newcomers), scaling with how much it's digesting. A structural brake on runaway magnets. 0 = off.
Famine
Runaway-leader brake

Make a civilization whose population has run far ahead of the field a less attractive destination for cross-civ migration. It is a self-correcting brake on a runaway leader that grows with its lead (0 off / 8 gentle / 15 standard / 28 strong). It never impedes the leader's OUTflow or internal moves. 0 = off.
Runaway-leader brake starts at

How far a civilization's population may run ahead of the world-average civilization before the anti-snowball headwind starts to bite, as a multiple of fair share. Lower = the brake engages sooner (more egalitarian); higher = only an extreme runaway leader is slowed.
Cultural enclaves

When a foreign diaspora grows into an established community in one of your cities, offer a one-time choice (embrace, tax, or let be) with a small yield reward and drawback, and track a persistent per-city enclave that turns "contested" (its yield benefit is reduced and it adds a small happiness strain) while you are at war with its homeland. Off = no enclave decisions or contested strain.
Share of a city needed to form
How much of a city a single foreign origin must make up before it can become a Cultural Enclave. Higher = rarer enclaves, as fewer cities ever qualify.
Smallest community that can form

The smallest standing population (in city-size points) a single foreign origin must reach before it can form a Cultural Enclave, so a tiny community can't qualify on share alone. Lower = small settlements can host enclaves too.
Stickiness
Movement between civilizations

How willing people are to leave one civilization for another, refugees included.[BLIST][LI][B]0%[/B]: people stay within their own civilization, even in a crisis; small civilizations keep their people.[LI][B]50%[/B] (default): moderate. In testing, the biggest gainer ended about 18% larger after 30 turns than without the mod.[LI][B]100%[/B]: people move almost freely; the biggest gainer ended about 37% larger.[/BLIST]
Refugees from conflict (overall)
Moves both sliders below at once (major-power wars and minor-power raids). It shows their average and shifts both by the same amount, so any gap you set between them is kept. 50% is the default.
Refugees from major-power wars

How strongly combat and sieges drive people out of a city when a major civilization is among the attackers.[BLIST][LI][B]0%[/B]: war creates no pressure to leave (hunger and unhappiness still do).[LI][B]50%[/B] (default): the standard war balance.[LI][B]100%[/B]: twice the pressure, so larger refugee waves.[/BLIST]
Refugees from minor-power raids

How strongly attacks by city-states and Independent Powers drive people out, when no major civilization takes part.[BLIST][LI][B]0%[/B]: raids create no pressure to leave.[LI][B]50%[/B] (default): a raid counts for less than half of a war.[LI][B]100%[/B]: a raid counts the same as a war at the default setting.[/BLIST]
In a crisis: shelter at home

How strongly people fleeing a war or disaster prefer another settlement of their own civilization over fleeing abroad. Most displacement is internal, and a high value keeps a refugee wave at home unless the homeland has nothing to offer. 0 sends them wherever the pull is strongest.
Shelter at home
Small-civilization brake

Slows people leaving a civilization for other civilizations once its population falls below the share of the average civilization set below. Stronger = small civilizations keep more of their people; 0 = off.
Small-civilization brake applies below
The share of the average civilization's population below which the small-civilization brake applies.
Put down roots
A community whose enclave stands in a settlement sends fewer of its people home through return migration. Stronger = fewer return; Off = they return at the normal rate.

How strongly a foreign community that has reached a foothold resists blending into the host, so it can grow into a full enclave instead of being absorbed first. Stronger = enclaves form more readily; Off = communities integrate at the normal rate and rarely reach the enclave threshold.
Time an enclave must last before it is recognized

How many turns a community must stay established before its enclave is recognized and the one-time stance decision is offered. The enclave itself, with its tile, appears as soon as the community is established; a brief spike (such as a war-refugee wave that later moves on) fades again without ever being recognized. A short dip below the threshold is forgiven. 0 = recognize as soon as the enclave forms.
Time between enclave decisions
Minimum turns between two Cultural Enclave decisions. Higher = the offers are spaced further apart.
Most enclaves per age
The most Cultural Enclaves one civilization can form in a single age, by decision or automatically. Lower = fewer enclaves each age.
Pace formation across each age

While a civilization has formed fewer enclaves this age than the target, its formation bars (share, size, and settling time) fall in step with the age's progress, down to the maximum reduction. They return to full once an enclave forms. The cap above still closes the age. Off = the plain bars all age long.
Enclaves aimed for per age
How many enclaves per civilization per age the pacing works toward. 1 makes at least one an age likely. 0 = no catch-up.
Most the requirements are lowered
The largest reduction of the formation bars the pacing applies late in an age with no enclave formed. 40% means the bars read 60% of their configured values.

Community large enough in any city

A foreign community with at least this many population points is established at any share of the settlement. Large cities can therefore host enclaves. The number scales with settlement size in this game. It applies as written when settlements average eighteen people, and moves in proportion, from half to double, as cities grow through the ages. An enclave fades only while its community is below both the fade share and this number. Off = share only.
Share below which an enclave fades

When its people's share of the settlement stays below this for the fade period, the enclave dissolves. The tile is removed and the chronicle records it. The default is half the foothold share, so a community that shrinks but persists keeps its enclave. Never = enclaves are permanent.

Emigration

Emigration moves population between settlements. Each turn, people leave unhappy, struggling or war-torn settlements for happier, more prosperous ones, within your civilization and across borders.[n][n]A Prosperity model scores each city on its happiness, yields and circumstances, weighted by distance so migration stays regional. A civilization pays an integration cost while its newcomers settle in.[n][n]Every settlement records the civilizations its people descend from, shown on the map by the Ethnic Composition lens. Newcomers gradually take on their host's identity, diasporas return home once their homeland recovers, and the Migration Chronicle records the great waves as history.[n][n]Aggressor avoidance, border policies, disasters, ethnic integration, return migration and refugee decisions are on by default; each can be switched off in Options, Add-ons, Emigration.
Common Questions

What drives migration. Most of it is tunable in Options, Add-ons, Emigration, and the dashboard's Guide tab has the full version.[n][n]✓ Your civilization and every other major civilization move population, met or unmet.[n]✗ City-states, minor civilizations and Independent Powers neither send nor receive population.[n]✓ Pushes: unhappiness, low yields, war damage, sieges (including attacks by a city-state or Independent Power), pillaging, starvation, plague, disasters and overcrowding.[n]✓ Pulls: prosperity, high happiness, a Pro-Immigration Stance, Open Borders and proximity.[n]✓ Migrants travel for a delay that grows with distance, and their host pays a temporary integration cost. War empties a city only by capturing it.[n]✓ Each settlement gains and loses at most a set number of people per turn, scaled by the intensity preset. Arrivals over the cap wait in transit, and refugees with nowhere to land die on the road.[n][n]Emigration leaves AI decisions and base-game files as they are. Unmet civilizations are simulated and stay hidden until you meet them.
Prosperity & Migration

Each settlement's Prosperity comes from its per-capita yields and, above all, its net happiness. An unhappy city loses people to happier, wealthier ones even in peacetime, and a small penalty for size limits how strongly a large city attracts.[n][n]People prefer nearby destinations, so migration spreads outward across a region. War, siege, starvation, unrest and disaster sharply lower a city's Prosperity and make it a source of refugees.
War & Refugees

A city sends war refugees while there is fighting inside its borders, damage to its districts, or pillaging on its land. The longer a siege lasts, the more people it drives out, and a remnant always stays until the city is captured.[n][n]Refugees flee away from the nearest invader. With aggressor avoidance on, they prefer their own civilization, then any neutral power, and choose the aggressor only as a last resort.[n][n]Migrants spend a few turns in transit, and each city takes in a limited number per turn; the rest wait and try again, longest-waiting first. If their destination is captured or razed while they travel, or stays too full to receive them, they die in transit and count as losses.[n][n]Once a homeland is at peace with the host and prospering again, some of its people abroad return home over time. When a great wave, driven by a neighbour's conquests or a plague, reaches your lands, you are occasionally asked how to receive it: take them in, settle them on the frontier, or turn them away. These refugee decisions can be switched off in Options.
Integration & the Cost of Growth

Each newcomer adds an integration load to the receiving civilization, which pays Gold and Happiness each turn until the load fades over the integration period. A civilization busy settling arrivals also becomes a less attractive destination, which keeps any one civilization from drawing in the world's migrants.[n][n]Integration also has a slower, cultural side. Over many turns, newcomers take on their host civilization's identity in each settlement's ethnic makeup, so a peaceful city gradually absorbs a diaspora. War with the diaspora's homeland, or unrest in the city, holds integration back, and the community keeps its own colour on the Ethnic Composition lens.
Borders & Influence

Your immigration stance is a policy card, available in every age. The Pro-Immigration Stance raises immigration and earns Influence each turn. The Anti-Immigration Stance lowers immigration and the number of your people leaving for rivals, adds Production in every city, and costs Influence each turn.[n][n]An Open Borders agreement increases migration in both directions between the two civilizations.
Attraction & Asylum

Talent Attraction, Cultural Magnetism and Commercial Draw turn immigration into yields: each newcomer adds to a Science, Culture or Gold bonus that grows while people keep arriving and fades when they stop.[n][n]The asylum policies, Selective Asylum and Refugee Compact, draw refugees fleeing war and disaster toward you, the most desperate first, and pay Influence each turn; Refugee Compact also pays Culture.
Talent Raids

From the diplomacy screen you can aim a Talent Raid, Cultural Offensive or Commercial Offensive at a rival. While it runs you pay Influence each turn, and that rival's migration tilts toward your cities. Each person who arrives pays the matching Science, Culture or Gold bonus, as a willing immigrant does.[n][n]These diplomatic actions come from the Diplomacy Extended mod and appear when it is installed.
Disasters & Plague

Floods, volcanoes, plagues and other disasters drive people out of stricken cities as disaster refugees. The worse the event, the harder it pushes.[n][n]Plague also travels with migrants: refugees from an infected city can seed a smaller outbreak where they settle.
When There Is No Refuge

When a city under siege, starving or struck by disaster has nowhere safe for its people to go, its trapped population dies or scatters, and the city loses population with no destination.[n][n]Even with somewhere to flee, a lethal crisis kills some who cannot escape in time. These losses start small, grow the longer the crisis lasts, and ease once it lifts, so a sudden blow is survivable and a grinding siege or famine wears a city down. They are uncapped: a long enough catastrophe can take a city's whole rural population, while its urban districts and the settlement itself hold until capture.[n][n]Only a city in crisis takes these losses. They are counted as deaths, separately from refugees who reach a new home.
Leaders & Civilizations

Some leaders and civilizations have small migration adjustments that reflect their history. They apply while per-civilization tuning is on, as it is by default.[n][n]Leaders whose happiness would otherwise make their cities dominant migration magnets attract a little less: Benjamin Franklin most, then Isabella, Ashoka and Rizal. Isabella and Xerxes pay more to integrate the people they conquer.[n][n]Pachacuti and, most of all, the Abbasids feel less overcrowding pressure in their dense cities. Confucius, the Han and the Qing keep more of their citizens, and the Khmer feel less of their non-capital unhappiness. The Normans and the English hold their population through a siege far better than others.
Scope & Visibility

Emigration simulates every living major civilization from the first turn, met or unmet, so migration follows the real state of the world and a city you later conquer carries the true origin history of its people.[n][n]By default the dashboard, graphs and map lenses show only civilizations you have met. The shared analytics-visibility setting (the same one the Demographics mod uses) chooses between your own civilization only, met civilizations, or all.[n][n]Simulation scope (whole world or met only) and on-screen visibility are separate settings.
Reading the Dashboard

Open the Migration dashboard from its button on the in-game dock, or from the Migration page in the Demographics mod. Its tabs:[n][n]• Network: an animated map of civilizations and their settlements, sized by how much population moves through them, with dots travelling the routes, flow arrows, and a timeline you can scrub.[n]• Net Migration (Table): arrivals, departures and net change by civilization, internal and external, beside refugees and losses.[n]• Causes: why people move, by cause, with the named wars, disasters and crises beneath each.[n]• Policies: who has adopted a Pro- or Anti-Immigration Stance.[n]• My Cities: your settlements ranked by how close each is to losing people, with each one's pressures.[n]• Diversity: the most diverse settlements and the make-up of their people.[n]• Notifications: the log of every notification, including the Migration Chronicle's entries.[n]• Guide: a quick reference of what drives migration.[n][n]On the map, the Prosperity lens (Shift+P) and the Ethnic Composition lens (Shift+E) paint each settlement tile by tile; see Map Lenses.
Ethnicity & Integration

Every settlement records the civilizations its people descend from and keeps that record through conquest. The Ethnic Composition lens (Shift+E) shows it as a per-tile mosaic: the urban core in the dominant origin's colour, smaller communities across its other tiles, and the exact mix in each settled tile's tooltip.[n][n]Newcomers gradually integrate into their host civilization; war with their homeland or unrest in the city keeps a community distinct. Once a homeland is at peace with its host and prospering again, return migration draws some of its people back home. All of this is on by default and can be switched off in Options.
Cultural Enclaves

A foreign community of at least 3 population points that holds 30% of a settlement, or the size bar (6 points at average settlement size), forms a Cultural Enclave in that city, yours or an AI's: a tile at the city's edge named for the origin people, carrying its own yield from the day it forms. After a dwell period the enclave is recognized. Each people has two stances drawn from its character. By default the city takes the first it can afford, and the Chronicle records it. With enclave recognition set to Ask me in Advanced settings, a pop-up with a quotation in that people's voice lets you pick a stance or none. A stance pays once, when chosen: Culture toward your current civic, Science toward your current research, Influence, or Gold, worth three turns of your income of that yield. A stance that pays anything but Gold costs two turns of your Gold income.[n][n]Each origin civilization can hold at most two enclaves in your empire, and at most three enclaves form in your empire per age. An enclave can change hands as the city's population shifts, and dissolves when its community stays below 12.5% of the settlement and below the size bar for 12 turns. At war with its homeland, an enclave is contested: it strains your happiness until peace, and a stance chosen meanwhile pays half. A community with an enclave rarely returns home on its own; see Calling Your People Home.
The Chronicle & Refugee Decisions

The Migration Chronicle records the world's great migrations as short history: a city emptied by war or disaster, a diaspora taking root far from home, a people returning once their homeland recovered, an enclave recognized or faded, a call home answered or unanswered. Its entries appear in the dashboard's Notifications tab.[n][n]When a real upheaval, a neighbour conquering several cities in a short span or a plague crisis, sends a wave of refugees toward your lands, you are asked how to receive them:[n]• Welcome them in: costs Gold and briefly strains your people; they settle among you.[n]• Settle them on the frontier: a smaller cost; they go to a smaller town.[n]• Turn them away: costs Influence.[n]Each decision carries a quotation in the voice of the people at your gates. At most two come per age, at least eighteen turns apart, and they can be switched off in Options. A civilization you have not met is named only as hearsay.

"In July, 1889, I left Oroomiah with not more than what amounts to five dollars in the United States, and not knowing where I should finally land." Isaac Adams, of Urmia, Persia by a Persian (1900)

"Woe is me, I have been exiled from the city, I can find no rest… I am sitting as if a stranger with head high in a strange city." Ningal, queen of Ur, mourning her people, Lament for Ur, lines 306-308 (early 2nd millennium BCE, trans.)
"Nikodemo conducted his fugitive fellow-Christians to Entare, who hospitably received them owing to his former friendship with Nikodemo." Robert P. Ashe, Chronicles of Uganda (1894)

"I remembered the proverb of our forefathers, which they used to sing, "You who stagger about under your burdens, those who come after you will be filled with amazement."" Ham Mukasa, Uganda's Katikiro in England (1904, trans. Millar)

"…дето нас млади пропъди / по тази тежка чужбина – / да ходим да се скитаме / немили, клети, недраги! (…that drove us out, still young, into this hard foreign land, to wander about unloved, wretched, unwanted!)" Hristo Botev, On Parting in 1868 (trans.)
"Баща и сестра и братя мили / аз да прегърна искам без злоба (Father and sister and dear brothers: I long to embrace them, without bitterness.)" Hristo Botev, To My Mother (1867, trans.)
"Non ignara mali, miseris succurrere disco. (O, I am wise in sorrow, and I help all suffering souls!)" Dido, in Virgil, Aeneid I (trans. Williams)

"And he set forth with sixty ships of fifty oars, and a multitude of men and women, to the number of thirty thousand, and with wheat and other provisions." Periplus of Hanno (5th c. BC, trans. Schoff)

"வள்ளியோர்ப் படர்ந்து, புள்ளின் போகி, / ‘நெடிய’ என்னாது சுரம்பல கடந்து, / … / பிறர்க்குத் தீதறிந் தன்றோ? இன்றே; (Seeking the generous, going like birds, never saying 'too far', crossing many wastelands … does this life of wandering for gifts know how to harm others? It does not.)" Kovur Kizhar, Purananuru 47 (trans.)

"彼中人物，昔甚繁華，時遷事變，畧無遺迹，惟我一人，知而道之。非夢而何？ (The people of that land were once in full flower; times shifted and things changed, and scarcely a trace remains. I alone know them and tell of them. What is this, if not a dream?)" Hồ Nguyên Trừng, Nam Ông mộng lục, preface (1438, trans.)
"一別家山恰十年 … 干戈未息幸身全 (Ten years exactly since I parted from my home hills … the fighting has not ceased; by good fortune I am still whole.)" Nguyễn Trãi, On Reaching Côn Sơn After the Turmoil (trans.)

"O God, whosoever thou art that didst ordain this flight, show mercy and bring me to the Residence! Peradventure thou wilt grant me to see the place where my heart dwelleth." Sinuhe, The Story of Sinuhe (trans. Gardiner)

"I thank the lord Serapis that, when I was in peril in the sea, he saved me immediately. … And it is well with me." Apion, an Egyptian in the Roman fleet, letter home, BGU II 423 (2nd c., trans. Strachan)
"How great a thing is it that my body should be embalmed in the land where I was born! To return there is happiness." Sinuhe, The Story of Sinuhe (trans. Griffith)

"…hrēran mid hondum hrīmcealde sǣ, wadan wræclāstas. Wyrd bið ful ārǣd. (…to stir with his hands the rime-cold sea, to tread the paths of exile. Fate is wholly fixed.)" the wanderer, The Wanderer, Exeter Book (10th c., trans.)

"monað modes lust mæla gehwylce ferð to feran, þæt ic feor heonan elþeodigra eard gesece. (The mind's desire urges my spirit every hour to journey, that far from here I should seek the land of foreign peoples.)" the seafarer, The Seafarer, Exeter Book (10th c., trans.)
"L’exil n’est pas une chose matérielle, c’est une chose morale. (Exile is not a material thing; it is a moral one.)" Victor Hugo, Ce que c'est que l'exil (1875, trans.)

"Guernesey est faite pour ne laisser au proscrit que de bons souvenirs ; mais l’exil existe en dehors du lieu d’exil. (Guernsey is made to leave the exile nothing but good memories; but exile exists outside the place of exile.)" Victor Hugo, Ce que c'est que l'exil (1875, trans.)

"Quand reverray-je, helas, de mon petit village / Fumer la cheminee (When shall I see again, alas, the chimney smoke rising from my little village…)" Joachim du Bellay, Les Regrets XXXI (1558, trans.)

"Heureux qui, comme Ulysse, a fait un beau voyage … Et puis est retourné, plein d'usage et raison, / Vivre entre ses parents le reste de son aage ! (Happy the man who, like Ulysses, has made a fine voyage … and then has come home, full of experience and good sense, to live among his kin the rest of his days!)" Joachim du Bellay, Les Regrets XXXI (1558, trans.)

"…omnibus Gallis idem esse faciendum quod Helvetii fecerint, ut domo emigrent, aliud domicilium, alias sedes, remotas a Germanis, petant. (…the Gauls must all do the same thing that the Helvetii had done, emigrate from their country, and seek another dwelling place, other settlements remote from the Germans.)" Diviciacus the Aeduan, Caesar, De Bello Gallico 1.31 (c. 50 BCE, trans.)

"Bellovesum ac Segovesum sororis filios impigros iuvenes missurum se esse in quas di dedissent auguriis sedes. (He signified his intention of sending his sister's sons Bellovesus and Segovesus, both enterprising young men, to settle in whatever locality the gods should by augury assign to them.)" Livy, on King Ambigatus sending out the Gauls, Ab Urbe Condita 5.34 (late 1st c. BCE, trans.)

"故國荒凉忍可思。不如忘却故憨癡。 (The old country lies desolate; how can I bear to think of it? Better to forget it, and play the fool on purpose.)" Yi Kyu-bo, Eok gu-gyeong sam-yeong, in Dongguk Yi Sangguk hujip (c. 1233-41, trans.)
"扁舟漂泊若爲情。四海誰云盡弟兄。 (Adrift in a little boat; how am I to bear it? Who was it said that within the four seas all men are brothers?)" Yi Je-hyeon, Sagwi, in Ikchae nango (1316, trans.)

"…they knew they were pilgrimes, & looked not much on those things, but lift up their eyes to ye heavens, their dearest cuntrie, and quieted their spirits." William Bradford, Of Plimoth Plantation (1620s)
"I never wish to have a better home than I got at present. Thank God, I am well and hearty, and hope that I shall remain so." John Stedman, labourer, from Upper Canada, letter home (1832)
"Fair these broad meads – these hoary woods are grand; / But we are exiles from our fathers’ land." Canadian Boat-Song (anon., 1829)

"My heart's in the Highlands, my heart is not here, / My heart's in the Highlands, a-chasing the deer; / Chasing the wild-deer, and following the roe, / My heart's in the Highlands, wherever I go." Robert Burns, My Heart's in the Highlands (1789)

"Oh, to be in England / Now that April's there, / And who wakes in England / Sees, some morning, unaware, / That the lowest boughs and the brush-wood sheaf / Round the elm-tree bole are in tiny leaf" Robert Browning, Home-Thoughts, from Abroad (1845)

"ὑπερημίσεας τῶν ἀστῶν ἔλαβε πόθος τε καὶ οἶκτος τῆς πόλιος καὶ τῶν ἠθέων τῆς χώρης (…more than half of the citizens were overcome with longing and pitiful sorrow for the city and the life of their land…)" Herodotus, on the Phocaeans, Histories I.165 (trans. Godley)

"καὶ ξυνέβη μοι φεύγειν τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἔτη εἴκοσι μετὰ τὴν ἐς Ἀμφίπολιν στρατηγίαν (It was also my fate to be an exile from my country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis…)" Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War V.26 (trans. Crawley)

"Κύμην Αἰολίδα προλιπών, ἐν νηὶ μελαίνῃ· οὐκ ἄφενος φεύγων οὐδὲ πλοῦτόν τε καὶ ὄλβον, ἀλλὰ κακὴν πενίην, τὴν Ζεὺς ἄνδρεσσι δίδωσιν· νάσσατο δʼ ἄγχʼ Ἑλικῶνος (…he left Aeolian Cyme and fled, not from riches and substance, but from wretched poverty which Zeus lays upon men, and he settled near Helicon…)" Hesiod, of his father, Works and Days (trans. Evelyn-White)

"My dear limbs yearn not to stay in the sacred streets of Cyme, but rather my great heart urges me to go unto another country, small though I am." Homeric Epigram IV (attr. Homer, trans. Evelyn-White)

"θάλαττα θάλαττα (Presently they could hear the soldiers shouting and passing on the joyful word, "The sea! the sea!")" Xenophon, of the Ten Thousand sighting the road home, Anabasis IV.7 (trans. Dakyns)

"ἰὼ πατρῷον οὖδας Ἀργείας χθονός, / δεκάτου σε φέγγει τῷδ᾽ ἀφικόμην ἔτους (All hail, soil of Argos, land of my fathers! On this happy day in the tenth year I have come to you. Many hopes have shattered, one only have I seen fulfilled.)" the Herald, in Aeschylus, Agamemnon 503-505 (trans. Smyth)
"人情同於懷土兮，豈窮達而異心？ (All human hearts alike long for their native soil; would hardship or success make any heart differ?)" Wang Can, Rhapsody on Climbing the Tower (c. 208, trans.)
"雖信美而非吾土兮，曾何足以少留？ (Though truly beautiful, this is not my own land; how could I bear to linger here even a little while?)" Wang Can, Rhapsody on Climbing the Tower (c. 208, trans.)

"使先至者安樂而不思故鄉，則貧民相募而勸往矣。 (Let those who arrive first live in peace and contentment, not pining for their old homes, and the poor will call one another to follow and gladly go.)" Chao Cuo, memorial on settling new lands (2nd c. BC, trans.)
"歸去來兮，田園將蕪胡不歸？ (Home! Let me go home! My fields and garden are going to weeds; why not return?)" Tao Yuanming, Return Home (405, trans.)

"The poor Hawaiians, strangers on their native soil, excluded from their own halls of legislation, have had their experience; alas, a bitter one." Liliʻuokalani, Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen (1898)
"…they return to their parents, but I was returned into tears; for I have no home, neither father nor mother." Henry ʻŌpūkahaʻia, Memoirs of Henry Obookiah (1818)
"Oh! how I want to see Owhyhee! But I think I never shall…" Henry ʻŌpūkahaʻia, Memoirs of Henry Obookiah (1818)

"こちふかはにほひおこせよ梅の花あるしなしとて春をわするな (When the east wind blows, send me your fragrance, plum blossoms; though your master is gone, do not forget the spring.)" Sugawara no Michizane, on leaving for exile, Shūi Wakashū (901, trans.)

"わたのはらやそしまかけてこきいてぬと人にはつけよあまのつり舟 (O'er the wide, wide sea, / Towards its many distant isles, / Rowing I set forth. / This, to all the world proclaim, / O ye boats of fisher-folk!)" Ono no Takamura, on his banishment, Kokin Wakashū (838, trans. MacCauley)

"昔男ありけり。京にありわびて。あづまへゆきけるに。…いとゝしく過行かたの戀しきにうらやましくもかへる浪哉 (Once there was a man who, finding life in the capital hard to bear, went east … 'Ever more I long for the places I have passed; how I envy the waves that go back.')" The Tales of Ise, section 7 (10th c., trans.)
"京にはをらじ。あづまのかたにすむべき所もとめにとてゆきけり。 (Resolved not to stay in the capital, he set off toward the East to find a place where he might live.)" The Tales of Ise, section 9 (10th c., trans.)

"ひさかたの月におひたるかつら川そこなる影もかはらざりけり (Katsura River, sprung from the laurel in the moon: even the reflection in your depths is just as it was.)" Ki no Tsurayuki, on the last night of the voyage home, Tosa Diary (935, trans.)

"天の原 ふりさけ見れば 春日なる みかさの山に 出でし月かも (When I look abroad o'er the wide-stretched Plain of Heaven, is the moon the same that on Mount Mikasa rose, in the land of Kasuga?)" Abe no Nakamaro, in China, before the voyage home, Kokin Wakashū 406 (trans. MacCauley)
"名にしおはゝいさこととはん都鳥我思ふ人は有やなしやと (If you are true to your name, then let me ask you, capital-bird: the one I love, is she living still, or not?)" The Tales of Ise, section 9 (10th c., trans.)

"Þótt þú langförull legðir / sérhvert land undir fót, / bera hugur og hjarta / samt þíns heimalands mót (Though, far-traveller, you set foot on every land, your mind and heart still bear the stamp of your homeland.)" Stephan G. Stephansson, Andvökur (trans.)

"Svo var haldið djúpt, að um morguninn sá ég Tjörnes, það seinasta af ættjörðu minni. (We held out to sea, so that in the morning I saw Tjörnes, the last of my native land.)" Guðmundur Stefánsson, letter on emigrating (1873, trans.)

"Hér fengum við svo góðar móttökur að þær gátu ekki verið betri, þó við hefðum komið til vina okkar á Íslandi eftir margra ára útlegð. (Here we received so good a welcome that it could not have been better, even had we come to our friends in Iceland after many years of exile.)" Guðmundur Stefánsson, letter on emigrating (1873, trans.)
"Trocósenos el reinar en vasallaje (We are turned from rulers into vassals.)" the Inca nobles of Cuzco, in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609, trans. Markham)

"forzado del amor natural de patria, me ofrecí al trabajo de escribir estos Comentarios (…influenced by a natural love of my country, I undertook the task of writing these Commentaries.)" Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales, proem (1609, trans. Markham)

"有人在田間。望之痛哭曰。國家棄我去。我輩何恃而生也。 (A man out in the fields watched them go, and wept bitterly: the state has abandoned us and gone; on what shall we rely to live?)" Yu Seong-ryong, on the flight from Seoul, Jingbirok (c. 1604, trans.)

"北風吹我如飛雪。南抵康津賣飯家。 (The north wind blows me along like driven snow, south as far as Gangjin, to a house that sells meals.)" Jeong Yak-yong, on reaching his place of exile, Gaekjung seohoe, in Yeoyudang jeonseo (1801, trans.)
"因屢與暹人交兵，遂至皆成曠地。 (As a result of repeated wars with the Siamese the land has been completely laid to waste.)" Zhou Daguan, Zhenla fengtuji (c. 1300, trans.)

"bhūtapūrvam abhūtapūrvaṃ vā janapadaṃ paradeśāpavāhanena svadeśābhiṣyandavamanena vā niveśayet (He should settle the countryside, whether previously settled or not, either by drawing population away from foreign lands or by draining off the surplus of his own.)" Kauṭilya, Arthaśāstra 2.1.1 (Mauryan tradition, received text c. 2nd c., trans.)

"कश्चित्कान्ताविरहगुरुणा स्वाधिकारात्प्रमत्तः शापेनास्तङ्गमितमहिमा वर्षभोग्येण भर्तुः (An erring Yaksha made his hapless home, / Doomed by his master humbly to abide, / And spend a long, long year of absence from his bride.)" Kalidasa, The Cloud-Messenger I.1 (trans. Ryder)
"Have pity on us, our brother, since we are all stretched on the shore of the ocean without seeing our hills and plains." the Kaqchikel ancestors, Annals of the Cakchiquels (16th c., trans. Brinton)

"There are your hills and plains; there, beyond the ocean, are your hills and plains, oh you my sons, there it is that you shall lift up your faces." the Obsidian Stone, to the Kaqchikel ancestors, Annals of the Cakchiquels (16th c., trans. Brinton)
"石をもて追はるるごとく / ふるさとを出でしかなしみ / 消ゆる時なし (As though driven out with stones, I left my home village, and that sorrow never fades.)" Ishikawa Takuboku, A Handful of Sand (1910, trans.)
"ふるさとの訛なつかし / 停車場の人ごみの中に / そを聴きにゆく (Longing for the accent of my home province, I go to the crowded railway station to hear it spoken.)" Ishikawa Takuboku, A Handful of Sand (1910, trans.)

"Yokohama deru tok'ya / Namida de deta ga / Ima ja ko mo aru / Mago mo aru (When I left Yokohama, I left in tears; but now I have children, and grandchildren too.)" holehole bushi, a Hawaii plantation song (Meiji-era emigrants, trans.)
"Adiós mi madre querida, … Yo me voy al extranjero, / Donde no hay revolución. (Goodbye, my dear mother, … I am going abroad, where there is no revolution.)" El Deportado (corrido, 1920s, trans.)

"Voy a contarles señores, / Todo lo que yo sufrí. / Desde que dejé mi patria, / Por venir a este país. (Let me tell you, gentlemen, all that I have suffered since I left my homeland to come to this country.)" El Deportado (corrido, 1920s, trans.)

"有弟皆分散，無家問死生。寄書長不達，況乃未休兵。 (My brothers are all scattered; there is no home where I might ask if they live or die. Letters sent never arrive, and still the fighting has not ceased.)" Du Fu, Thinking of My Brothers on a Moonlit Night (8th c., trans.)

"江水三千里，家書十五行。行行無別語，只道早歸鄉。 (The river runs three thousand li; the letter from home is fifteen lines. Line after line says nothing else, only: come home soon.)" Yuan Kai, Receiving a Letter from Home in the Capital (14th c., trans.)

"君自故鄉來，應知故鄉事。來日綺窗前，寒梅着花未。 (You have come from my home town, so you must know how things stand at home. The day you left, before the patterned window, had the winter plum yet come into flower?)" Wang Wei, Miscellaneous Poems II (8th c., trans.)
"露從今夜白，月是故鄉明。 (From tonight the dew turns white; the moon is brighter over my home.)" Du Fu, Thinking of My Brothers on a Moonlit Night (759, trans.)
"舉頭望明月，低頭思故鄉。 (I lift my head and gaze at the bright moon; I lower my head and think of home.)" Li Bai, Quiet Night Thought (8th c., trans.)

"Amid the gloom and horrors of the present separation, we are cheered with a hope that ere long we shall reach our destined land…" George W. Harkins, Choctaw chief, Farewell Letter to the American People (1832)
"I ask you in the name of justice, for repose for myself and for my injured people." George W. Harkins, Choctaw chief, Farewell Letter to the American People (1832)

"Some settled on one side of the River, some on the other. Those on one side are called Cussetaws, those on the other, Cowetas; yet they are one people…" Chekilli, Creek head chief, Kasihta migration legend (1735)
"My Daidu, where my fathers dwelt in joy and gladness, my faithful lords and princes, and my dear people." Toghon Temür (attr.), lament on leaving Daidu, 1368 (trans.)
"It passed through my mind that to wander from mountain to mountain, homeless and houseless, without country or abiding-place, had nothing to recommend it." Babur, Baburnama (trans. Beveridge)

"हातका मैला सुनका थैला, के गर्नु धनले ? साग र सिस्नु खाएको बेस आनन्दी मनले ! (Bags of gold are but dirt on the hands; what is wealth for? Better to eat greens and nettles, with a contented heart!)" Muna, to her husband bound for Lhasa, Laxmi Prasad Devkota, Muna Madan (1936, trans.)

"…inter extraneos, in magna egestate, nec sine multa formidine, educatus est (…brought up amongst foreigners in great indigence, and not without much apprehension.)" Orderic Vitalis, on the exiled William Clito, Historia ecclesiastica XII (trans. Forester)

"Bu gurbet câna gâyet kâr kıldı / Ki âlemden beni bîzâr kıldı (This exile has wrought so deeply on my soul that it has made me weary of the world.)" Cem Sultan, Divan, written in exile (15th c., trans.)

"O Raja of Rajas, give us a place in this city: we are strangers seeking protection who have arrived in thy town and place of residence." the Zoroastrian refugees, to the Rana of Sanjan, Qissa-i Sanjan (c. 1600, trans. Hodivala)

"بگذر ای باد دل‌افروز خراسانی / بر یکی مانده به یمگان دره زندانی (Pass by, O heart-kindling breeze of Khorasan, over one left behind, a prisoner in the valley of Yumgan.)" Nasir Khusraw, Divan, qasida 236 (11th c., trans.)

"در اقصای عالم بگشتم بسی / به سر بردم ایام با هر کسی / تمتع به هر گوشه‌ای یافتم / ز هر خرمنی خوشه‌ای یافتم (I wandered far through the farthest corners of the world and spent my days with every kind of people; in every corner I found some joy, from every harvest I gleaned an ear of grain.)" Saadi, Bustan, prologue (1257, trans.)

"غم غریبی و غربت چو بر نمی‌تابم / به شهر خود روم و شهریار خود باشم (Since I cannot bear the grief of being a stranger in a strange land, I will go to my own city and be my own sovereign.)" Hafez, Divan, ghazal 337 (14th c., trans.)

"Being now at liberty, though like Adam when he was first created, that is, naked and destitute… I determined to enter into the order of the pirates…" Alexandre Exquemelin, The Buccaneers of America (1684)

"Ich hatte einst ein schönes Vaterland. / Der Eichenbaum / Wuchs dort so hoch, die Veilchen nickten sanft. / Es war ein Traum. (Once I had a beautiful fatherland. The oak tree grew so tall there, the violets nodded gently. It was a dream.)" Heinrich Heine, In der Fremde (1844, trans.)

"Der Bootsmann winkt! – Zieht hin in Frieden: / Gott schütz’ euch, Mann und Weib und Greis! (The boatman beckons! Go forth in peace: God keep you, man and wife and greybeard!)" Ferdinand Freiligrath, Die Auswanderer (1838, trans.)

"Das sind dieselben Töpf’ und Krüge, / Oft an der Heimat Born gefüllt! (These are the same pots and jugs so often filled at the spring back home!)" Ferdinand Freiligrath, Die Auswanderer (1838, trans.)

"ای مرغ سحر چو این شب تار / بگذاشت ز سر سیاه‌کاری … یاد آر ز شمع مرده یاد آر (O bird of the morning, when this gloomy night puts aside its dark deeds… Remember, O remember, that extinguished Lamp!)" Ali-Akbar Dehkhoda, written in exile (1909, trans. Browne)

"憶別家鄉月幾圓 / 家人倚望音書勿 (Since I left my home village, how many times has the moon been full? My family leans at the door, watching for letters.)" a Chinese migrant from Taishan, Angel Island wall poem (trans.)

"litora cum patriae lacrimans portusque relinquo / et campos, ubi Troia fuit: feror exsul in altum (Through tears I saw recede my native shore, the haven and the plains where once was Troy. An exile on the seas … I took my way.)" Aeneas, in Virgil, Aeneid III (trans. Williams)

"Cum subit illius tristissima noctis imago, / qua mihi supremum tempus in urbe fuit … / labitur ex oculis nunc quoque gutta meis. (When the most sad remembrance recurs to me of that night, which was my last in the City … even now does the tear start from my eyes.)" Ovid, Tristia I.3, from exile (trans. Riley)

"uidebis maiorem partem esse quae relictis sedibus suis uenerit in maximam quidem ac pulcherrimam urbem, non tamen suam. (…you will find that the greater part of them have left their own abodes, and journeyed to a city which, though great and beauteous beyond all others, is nevertheless not their own.)" Seneca, Consolation to Helvia, from exile (trans. Stewart)

"o quid solutis est beatius curis, / cum mens onus reponit, ac peregrino / labore fessi venimus larem ad nostrum, / desideratoque acquiescimus lecto? (O what is more blessed than cares laid down, when the mind sets aside its burden, and, worn out by toil abroad, we come to our own hearth and rest at last in the bed we longed for?)" Catullus, Carmina XXXI, on reaching Sirmio (trans.)

"У зверя есть нора, у птицы есть гнездо. / Как бьётся сердце, горестно и громко, / Когда вхожу, крестясь, в чужой, наёмный дом / С своей уж ветхою котомкой! (The beast has its lair, the bird its nest. How my heart beats, grieving and loud, as I enter, crossing myself, a stranger's rented house with my worn-out knapsack!)" Ivan Bunin, in exile (1922, trans.)

"Тучки небесные, вечные странники! / … / Мчитесь вы, будто, как я же, изгнанники, / С милого севера в сторону южную. (Clouds of heaven, eternal wanderers! … You race on as if, like me, you were exiles, from the dear north toward the south.)" Mikhail Lermontov, Clouds, on leaving for exile (1840, trans.)
"汝や知る都は野辺の夕雲雀あがるを見ても落つる涙は (Do you know, evening skylark? The capital is now an open moor, and even as I watch you rise, my tears fall.)" Iio Tsunefusa, on Kyoto after the Ōnin War (15th c., trans.)
